title: Pentagon Confirms Firing Squad Execution of Fort Hood Shooter Will Be Livestreamed
snippet: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the upcoming execution of Fort Hood gunman Nidal Malik Hasan will be broadcast live, sparking fierce legal and ethical debate over military capital punishment.
content:
WASHINGTON — In an unprecedented move, the Pentagon confirmed Thursday that the upcoming firing squad execution of Fort Hood gunman Nidal Malik Hasan will be broadcast live to the public. The decision marks the first U.S. military execution in over six decades and follows recent comments from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth emphasizing transparency surrounding the event.

Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others during a 2009 mass shooting at the Texas military base. The U.S. Army announced earlier this week that his execution is scheduled for Dec. 3 at Fort Hood, following final authorization from President Donald Trump.

A Public Spectacle or Unfiltered Transparency?

Speaking to conservative news outlet Real America’s Voice News, Hegseth promised public visibility for the execution, stating, “We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public.” When asked whether Hasan had made any final requests or tried to contact the administration, the Pentagon chief dismissed the inquiry: “Don’t care. We’ll see him on Dec. 3.”

The plan to broadcast a violent form of capital punishment has ignited sharp disagreement among legal scholars and civil rights experts. Some question the government's underlying motivations, while others suggest public viewing could shed light on the realities of the death penalty.

Elisabeth Semel, co-director of the Death Penalty Clinic at UC Berkeley Law, raised severe concerns about turning capital punishment into a broadcast event. “This is a president who’s about spectacle and that’s, I think, precisely the message that he intends to deliver,” Semel said, adding that government-mandated livestreams present profound questions regarding human dignity and public policy.

On the other hand, Fordham University law professor Deborah Denno argued that streaming the event could foster institutional accountability. “I think it could possibly be a good idea because it would be transparent and the public would be fully aware that it’s happening,” Denno noted, though she acknowledged that strict regulations around platform hosting and age limits would be required.

Legal Hurdles and Historical Precedent

Despite the set date, military law specialists emphasize that Hasan could file a federal habeas corpus petition in civilian court, a process that could halt the proceedings indefinitely. Yale Law School visiting lecturer Eugene R. Fidell pointed out that legal challenges “might outlast the current administration,” leaving the matter in the hands of future leadership.

Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist who was paralyzed after being shot during his 2009 capture, largely engineered his own death sentence during his 2013 court-martial. Acting as his own attorney, he called no defense witnesses and offered no closing arguments. Leaked documents later revealed Hasan told mental health evaluators that he viewed execution as a path to martyrdom.

Hasan’s former attorney, John Galligan, raised additional concerns this week, alleging Army officials failed to ensure legal counsel was present when Hasan was formally notified of his execution date. Army representatives denied any wrongdoing, stating that repeated attempts were made to reach defense counsel and that Hasan’s right to communicate with his legal team remains completely unrestricted.

If executed as planned, Hasan will be the first service member put to death by the military since Army Pvt. John Bennett was hanged in 1961, and the first military execution by firing squad since World War II.
